newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Troubled Agrobanka readied for sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Troubled Agrobanka readied for sale.

text.p: The Czech central bank set out its plan on Friday to revive Agrobanka, the country's fifth largest bank, splitting the troubled institution's sound and questionable assets to allow the entry of a strategic investor.

The central bank said it was splitting the bank's assets into two parts -- questionable and sound -- allowing for the sound assets to be sold off in a tender while the questionable assets will be retained and "their value realised".

"It (the plan) allows...existing shareholders the opportunity to retain an interest in those assets against which substantial provisions are required by the auditors," central bank administrator Jiri Klumpar said in a statement.
"The recommended option fully meets the objectives of the administration," he added.
In September, Agrobanka, the fifth largest bank, went into forced administration because of low liquidity connected with the failure of a smaller Plzen-based bank, Kreditni Banka a.s..
The central bank is currently searching for a majority shareholder to take control of Agrobanka which was connected to Kreditni through an obscure investment firm called Motoinvest.
The failure of Kreditni, which investigators said was caused by dubious debt-swap deals linked to Motoinvest, in turn caused a crisis of confidence in Agrobanka.
The statement added that preparations for the internal reorganisation of the bank would start immediately, allowing for the rapid sale of the new division.

"The creation of a strong separate division of Agrobanka is likely to attract considerable interest from leading international commercial banks committed to the development of the Czech banking system," said John Sleeman, director of investment bank HSBC in Prague, which is arranging the tender.
Agrobanka has said that U.S. General Electric Capital Corp, and Austria's Raiffeisen bank, are among five bidders seeking a stake in the Prague-based bank through the tender.

Agrobanka was the largest fully-private financial institution in the country in terms of assets with 69.2 billion crowns ($2.4 billion) at the end of September. It posted a 372 million crown net profit in 1995, after 171 million in 1994.
Agrobanka is the 12th and the largest Czech bank to have been subjected to central bank intervention since post-Communist liberalisation of the sector created dozens of new banks in the early 1990s.

After a wave of collapses, the central bank drew up a plan under which an arm of the state-held Konsolidacni Banka would buy off doubtful assets from small banks at a nominal price for a certain period of time.
In exchange the banks had to adhere to strict rules and close central bank supervision.
